en: The *Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning* (*Yuktiṣaṣṭikā*),
composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven during the Chao-feng era.

I, the subject Shi Hu, a former Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and recipient of the purple robe, respectfully translate this by imperial decree: I take refuge in the Lord of Silence throughout the three times, Who proclaims the words of the True Dharma of dependent origination;
If one realizes that all phenomena are free from dependent origination, Then the Dharma practices one performs will likewise be free from it.
Free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, the wise have nothing on which to rely;
profound and without an object of perception, the meaning of dependent origination is established.
If one claims that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then various faults will arise.
The wise should, in accordance with reason, investigate whether phenomena possess intrinsic nature.
If an intrinsic nature were truly found, it would be as the ignorant conceptualize;
yet if there is no intrinsic nature, there is no cause—how then could the meaning of liberation be established?
One cannot say there is existence, nor can one say there is non-existence;
having realized both existence and non-existence, the one of great wisdom speaks in accordance with reality.
Do not view nirvāṇa and saṃsāra as being of different natures.
There is no distinction between the two natures of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra; both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are non-existent.
If one thoroughly understands saṃsāra, this itself is nirvāṇa.
The nature of birth-existence is refuted, and the same applies to the conceptualization of cessation;
like things produced by illusion, when cessation manifests, it has no reality.
If there were something to be destroyed in cessation, one would know that it is conditioned.
If even in the present life nothing is attained, how can one know of the destruction of phenomena?
Those aggregates do not cease; when defilement is exhausted, that is nirvāṇa.
If one thoroughly understands the nature of cessation, one attains liberation.
Whether as phenomena arising or phenomena ceasing, both are unfindable;
when observed by correct wisdom, they are seen to arise conditioned by ignorance.
If one sees that phenomena are quiescent, all conditioned activities are likewise so.
Knowing this most excellent Dharma, one attains boundless knowledge of phenomena.
The nature of dependent origination can be seen; this meaning is not without vision.
Within this, the subtle nature is not a conceptualization of dependent origination.
That which is spoken by the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is said not to be without cause;
if one exhausts the source of afflictions, one immediately shatters the marks of saṃsāra.
Regarding the definitive practice of all phenomena, one perceives that there is action and grasping.
What are the prior and subsequent limits, established through conditions?
How is it that what has already arisen before subsequently transforms again?
Therefore, the prior and subsequent limits are like what is seen by worldly illusions.
How can an illusion arise? How can there be attachment?
The deluded, within an illusion, seek that illusion as if it were real.
The prior limit is not the subsequent limit; because of clinging to views, one does not relinquish them.
When wisdom contemplates that nature is without intrinsic nature, it is like a phantom, a mirage, or a reflection.
If one claims that arising is not ceasing, this is a conceptualization of the conditioned.
Yet that wheel of dependent origination turns along without manifesting anything.
Whether already arisen or yet to arise, its intrinsic nature is non-arising;
if its intrinsic nature is non-arising, how can the name "arising" be applied?
Because quiescence is the exhaustion of phenomena, this exhaustion cannot be apprehended;
if intrinsic nature were inexhaustible, how could the designation "exhaustion" be established?
Not even the slightest phenomenon can arise, nor can the slightest phenomenon cease.
Those two paths of arising and ceasing manifest according to phenomena and according to meaning.
To know arising is to know ceasing; to know ceasing is to know impermanence.
If one knows the nature of impermanence, one will not find a bottom to any phenomena.
All phenomena arise from conditions; though they arise, they are immediately subject to cessation.
Like one who has reached the further shore, one perceives the true nature of the great ocean.
If one’s own mind does not understand this, ordinary beings cling to a self-nature.
The inversion of existence and non-existence gives rise to all faults.
All phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self;
therein one sees the departure from phenomena, and through wisdom observes the nature of existence and non-existence.
Without abiding and without an object of perception, It has no root and does not stand;
Born from the seed of ignorance, It is devoid of beginning, middle, or end.
The great evil city of delusive darkness Is as unsubstantial as a plantain tree.
Like a city of Gandharvas, all that is seen is a worldly illusion.
Regarding this realm, from its initial Brahmā, the Buddha has explained it according to reality;
subsequently, the various sages have not erred, and their explanations likewise show no difference.
The world is shrouded by delusion and flows on in a continuous stream of craving;
the wise understand all cravings and thus teach with equanimity.
First, they speak of the existence of all phenomena, and within that existence, they seek their true nature.
Later, even the seeking of nature is non-existent; thus, the nature of non-attachment is free from grasping.
If one does not understand the meaning of detachment, one will immediately become attached upon hearing [the teaching];
consequently, the meritorious deeds performed by such ordinary fools are self-destructive.
As previously explained with impartiality, those various karmas are real;
if their intrinsic nature is thoroughly understood, this teaching is that they are unborn.
All that I have thus spoken is based entirely upon the Buddha’s word and instruction.
Just as they have been proclaimed— the phenomena of the aggregates, bases, and elements,
the primary elements, and consciousness— all that which is taught is equal;
when that wisdom is directly realized, it is without error and without conceptual construction.
If this is as it truly is, the Buddha calls it nirvāṇa.
This is supreme and without falsehood; ignorance is mere conceptualization.
If the mind is distracted, it provides an opportunity for all the māras.
If one truly departs from faults, this is precisely that which is unarisen;
thus, the Buddha taught to the world that ignorance is the condition [for suffering].
If the world were without conceptual construction, how could it be unarisen?
If ignorance were extinguishable, then once extinguished it would not arise again;
for "arising" and "ceasing" are contradictory terms, yet the ignorant give rise to such conceptual discrimination.
Where there is a cause, there is arising; where there are no conditions, there is no abiding.
If that which is apart from conditions has an intrinsic nature, how could this existence be attained?
If there were an intrinsic nature to be grasped, one would say that arising and abiding exist;
herein, doubt is further multiplied, namely, that there is a dharma that can abide.
If awakening were something to be realized, it would be constantly spoken of everywhere;
if an abiding nature could be grasped, this teaching would still be subject to arising.
To claim that phenomena possess substantial reality is the speech of those lacking wisdom.
If one claims that dharmas have a location, even grasping cannot be found.
Dharmas are without arising and without self; wisdom awakens to and enters their true nature.
Characteristics such as permanence and impermanence all arise from the mind’s views.
If multiplicity were established, then the reality of desire would be established;
why then would that not lead to the fault of [desire] being eternal?
If unity were established, then what is desired would be like the moon in water.
Neither real nor unreal, all arise from the mind’s perceptions.
The dharmas of greed and hatred are extremely heavy; from these arise views and attachments.
Because of disputes, they are established as such; yet one clings to them as real, despite their lack of intrinsic nature.
Because of those causes, various views arise; because of views, afflictions are born.
If one understands this correctly, both views and afflictions will be exhausted.
One should know that phenomena are impermanent, appearing because they arise from conditions.
Dependent origination is itself without arising; this is the supreme word of truth.
Sentient beings, with their perverse and deluded intellects, perceive the unreal as real;
they give rise to disputes with others while their own conduct revolves in perversion.
If one's own portion cannot be established, how can another's portion exist?
Since both one's own and another's portions are absent, the wise understand this and have no disputes.
If there were even the slightest phenomenon upon which to rely, afflictions would be like venomous snakes.
If there is neither stillness nor movement, the mind has nothing upon which to rely.
Afflictions are like venomous snakes, giving rise to most grievous faults;
when one is shrouded by the poison of afflictions, how can one perceive the various states of mind?
Just as a fool beholds a reflection and falsely conceives of it as real, so too are the fetters of the world: wisdom is ensnared by delusion.
Nature is like a reflection; it is not within the range of the eye of ordinary knowledge.
Great wisdom is fundamentally unborn; it is the perception of subtle objects.
To be attached to form is called being an ordinary person; to be free from craving is to be a lesser sage.
To thoroughly understand the intrinsic nature of form—this is the supreme wisdom.
If one clings to various wholesome dharmas, it is like being free from greed and inversion;
yet, having seen them as like illusory persons, one is free from seeking their essential substance.
To know this meaning is to avoid error; one does not contemplate existence or non-existence.
Afflictions are unfindable; the light of intrinsic nature shatters false cognition.
Wisdom is pure through its freedom from defilement, yet there is no purity upon which it can rely;
for where there is reliance, there is defilement, and that very purity would give rise to further faults.
When one perceives that even the most evil afflictions are by nature detached,
the mind becomes free from agitation and one crosses the ocean of birth and death.
This nectar of the sublime Dharma arises from great compassion.
Proclaimed according to the words of the Tathāgata, it is free from limited conceptualization.
Herein, such things are difficult to express; yet for the wise, they are accomplished through their own vision.
As the wise observe and follow the various gateways, all of this proceeds from great compassion.
The true nature within all phenomena— The wise contemplate it accordingly and in accordance with reality.
From this, faith arises in those who turn toward it, And they uproot sentient beings, freeing them from all suffering.
This meaning is most profound and vast; for the sake of supreme benefit, I have praised and explained it.
Now that these words of great wisdom have been proclaimed, the darkness of delusion in both oneself and others can be utterly destroyed.
Having shattered that darkness of ignorance and afflictions, one acts in accordance with reality, free from demonic obstacles;
by this, one can open the gate to the happy realms—what loss could there be in the various matters of liberation?
Those who uphold the pure precepts attain rebirth in heaven; this is a definitive and true statement.
Even if one who has broken the precepts abides in a right mind, though their conduct is ruined, their view is not ruined.
The growth of seeds is not without purpose; seeing their benefit, one engages in extensive cultivation.
Without great compassion as the primary cause, how could a wise person give rise to the desire for the Dharma?
The Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning (Yuktiṣaṣṭikā)
